headline: Approved 2026/2027 school resource officer agreement and sent it forward for final approval.
summary: The committee discussed school resource officer staffing and training, class cutting, and student attendance data. It approved the school resource officer agreement and forwarded it for final approval. Attendance outreach to families is scheduled for August 31 through September 2.

decision_titles: 2026/2027 School Resource Officer Memorandum of Understanding
plain_text:
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
COMMITTEE ON STUDENT CONDUCT 
 
August 19, 2026 5:00 p.m.  
 
1. Chair Hamer called the meeting to order at 5:00 p.m. 
 
2. The Clerk called the roll.  
 
 Present: Committee Member Hamer, Want, Stewart, St. John and Taylor. 
 
 Absent: Committee Members Bergeron and Smith. 
 
 
3. Public Forum 
 
There was no one present to give public comment. 
 
 
6. Approval of the Minutes of the following meeting: June 17, 2026 
  
On motion of Committee Member Want, duly seconded by Committee Member Stewart, it was moved to 
approve the minutes of the June 17, 2026 meeting.  All were in favor and the motion passed. 
 
 
7. Presentations 
 
There were no presentations this evening. 
 
8. School Resource Officer Memorandum of Understanding (2026/2027) – by    
Dr. Kelly Espinola, Assistant Superintendent 
 
Dr. Espinola presented the updated Memorandum of Understanding regarding School Resource Officers. 
She explained that the financial portion of the agreement had previously been reviewed by the Finance 
and Facilities Committee and would be forwarded to the full Board for consideration.  She stated that 
there were very few changes to the agreement. The most significant change was contained in the section 
addressing SRO training.  Working with the Manchester Police Department, the District identified 
specific training areas that would now be explicitly included in the agreement. 
 
Questions and comments from the committee included:
August 19, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 2 of 9 
 
1. The District would continue to have 10 School Resource Officers.  The distribution was identified 
as follows: 
 one SRO at each middle school; 
 one SRO at Manchester School of Technology; 
 one SRO at West High School; 
 two SROs at Memorial High School; and 
 two SROs at Central High School. 
2. The Committee discussed language remaining in the agreement from earlier concerns raised in 
approximately 2022.  Dr. Espinola explained that many of those concerns had since been 
addressed through current practices and through other provisions in the agreement. She stated that 
principals are surveyed annually regarding the performance and responsibilities of their SROs. 
Principals also work closely with the Manchester Police Department and with the SRO assigned 
to their building. 
3. Dr. Espinola emphasized that serving as a police officer in a school environment is significantly 
different from traditional street policing and requires close collaboration with school 
administration. 
4. Committee Member Want asked whether SRO training requirements were documented and 
whether all SROs had completed the required training.  Dr. Espinola stated that training is 
documented by the Manchester Police Department and that she would confirm whether every 
SRO had completed all required training.  She noted that one SRO had recently attended a three-
day school-safety conference and that SROs also participate in active-threat and emergency drills. 
5. Committee Member Want stated that, while school-safety training was important, she was 
particularly concerned about training in areas such as: 
 ethics; 
 de-escalation; 
 student mental health; 
 student wellness; and 
 supporting student resilience. 
 
She emphasized the importance of ensuring that all SROs have the training necessary to establish 
positive relationships with students.
August 19, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 3 of 9 
 
6. Dr. Espinola stated that her understanding was that SROs complete training requirements both 
through the Manchester Police Department and through the Manchester School District, and she 
agreed to confirm the requirements and completion status. 
7. Committee Member Stewart asked whether all returning SROs would remain in their previous 
schools.  Dr. Espinola stated that she was aware of two new SROs who would be assigned to 
Central High School. 
 
On motion of Committee Member Want, duly seconded by Committee Member Taylor, it was moved to 
approve the 2026/2027 School Resource Officer Memorandum of Understanding and forward  this item 
to the full Board of School Committee for approval on August 24, 2026.  All were in favor and the motin 
passed. 
  
 
9. Quarterly Student Discipline Board Report – August 2026 – by Dr. Kelly     
Espinola, Assistant Superintendent 
 
Dr. Espinola presented the quarterly Student Discipline Report.   
 
Questions and comments from the committee included: 
1. Focusing much of its discussion on class cutting and student attendance. 
2. Committee Chair Hamer stated that concerns had been raised by members of the community and 
District staff regarding the number of class cuts occurring in the high schools. 
3. The Committee requested that, beginning with the new school year, the District review class-cut 
data and compare the 2026–2027 data with prior-year information. 
4. The Committee stated that the goal should not simply be to identify the number of cuts, but also to 
understand why students are not attending individual classes. 
5. Possible contributing factors discussed included: 
 family or home circumstances; 
 scheduling issues; 
 lack of engagement; 
 conflicts between a student and teacher; 
 curriculum concerns; and 
 other individual barriers.
August 19, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 4 of 9 
 
6. The Committee also discussed the impact of the revised ED 306 standards and competency-based 
education. 
7. Committee Chair Hamer noted that competency-based learning focuses on mastery rather than 
simply seat time, while also recognizing that regular class attendance remains important. 
 
 
10. 2025/2026 Attendance Data – by Dr. Kelly Espinola, Assistant Superintendent  
 
Dr. Espinola emphasized that the District expects students to attend class and receive instruction directly 
from educators.  She stated that administrators had identified cases in which students had more than 30 
absences in a class while still earning an A. 
 
Dr. Espinola explained that high school principals and assistant principals had developed a procedure to 
address this issue.  When a student accumulates three absences in a specific class during a quarter, access 
to the Google Classroom for that particular class may be paused.  The purpose is to create an opportunity 
for the student and teacher to have a direct conversation about the reason for the absences. 
 
Dr. Espinola explained that the meeting could help identify barriers such as: 
 scheduling concerns; 
 transportation or family obligations; 
 responsibility for getting younger siblings to school; 
 issues with a particular course; 
 or other circumstances affecting attendance. 
 
The District also planned to prevent tests and quizzes from being posted in Google Classroom. 
Administration stated that assessments should be administered directly to students rather than completed 
remotely without staff supervision. 
 
Questions and comments included: 
1. Committee Member Taylor clarified that the three absences referred specifically to absences from 
an individual class and not three full-day absences from school.  Dr. Espinola confirmed that only 
access to the Google Classroom associated with that particular class would be paused.
August 19, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 5 of 9 
 
2. Committee Member Want asked how the new procedure would be communicated to students and 
families.  Dr. Espinola stated that she had first wanted to present the proposal to the Committee 
and would then work with high school principals to develop consistent communication. 
3. Committee Member Stewart asked whether exceptions would be made for legitimate 
circumstances such as a student suffering from a prolonged illness.  Dr. Espinola stated that there 
would be a distinction between a student whose whereabouts and medical circumstances are 
known and a student who is cutting class without explanation. 
4. The Administration would work with principals and staff to apply the procedure reasonably. 
5. Dr. Espinola stated that the District would closely monitor class-cut data. She planned to bring 
September data to the Committee in October and compare the beginning of the 2026–2027 school 
year with the prior year. 
6. The Committee also discussed whether daily attendance reports should continue monthly or 
instead be presented quarterly. 
7. Dr. Espinola proposed shifting average daily attendance data to a quarterly report so that more 
attention could be given to class cuts.  The Committee agreed to try the quarterly schedule and 
revisit the format if necessary. 
8. Committee Member Taylor requested that administration examine whether class-cut trends were 
concentrated in particular: 
 courses; 
 subject areas; 
 schools; or 
 instructional situations. 
 
He noted that different patterns could require different responses. 
9. Committee Member Want agreed and stated that frequent cutting of a specific class could indicate 
disengagement or another school-based issue.  Dr. Espinola stated that she could provide general 
trends publicly but would not identify individual teachers in public reports.  
10. Any personnel-specific issues would be addressed administratively and privately. 
11. The Committee also noted that the issue could sometimes relate to curriculum rather than an 
individual teacher.  The Administration agreed to conduct a deeper analysis.
August 19, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 6 of 9 
 
12. Chair Hamer stated that it would also be useful to compare patterns across the District's high 
schools to determine whether the same issues are appearing consistently or whether individual 
schools have different patterns. 
13. Dr. Espinola announced an attendance outreach initiative scheduled for August 31, September 1, 
and September 2.  The Manchester School District, working with the Office of Youth Services, 
planned to identify students who had missed between 18 and 25 days of school during the prior 
year.  District and Office of Youth Services staff would conduct outreach to families and, when 
appropriate, visit homes to welcome students back and identify barriers preventing regular 
attendance.  Examples could include a student needing: 
 a class schedule; 
 information about school; 
 transportation assistance; 
 or another form of support. 
14. Dr. Espinola stated that the District wanted to reach students before they became truant.  She 
explained that students with significant absences are at increased risk of long-term academic 
difficulties.  The outreach effort would particularly focus on rising sixth-grade and ninth-grade 
students. 
15. The Administration stated that research identifies sixth grade as an important transition point and 
that students who are truant at that stage may face a greater risk of ultimately failing to graduate. 
16. Committee Member Taylor asked what follow-up would occur when families could not be 
reached during a home visit.  Dr. Espinola stated that the District would use a sequence of: 
1. telephone contact; 
2. home outreach; and 
3. follow-up email. 
17. The Committee expressed support for the initiative. 
18. Committee Member Want asked whether advisories, learning labs, and lunch periods were 
included in class-cut reporting.  Dr. Espinola stated that advisory attendance would be included 
because students receive credit for advisory.  She said she would confirm how learning labs and 
lunches would be treated.  She emphasized that, regardless of academic credit, the District has a 
school-safety responsibility to know where students are throughout the day, particularly in the 
event of an emergency or evacuation.
August 19, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 7 of 9 
 
2025–2026 Attendance Data 
Dr. Espinola presented average daily attendance data for the 2025–2026 school year.   Manchester's 
average daily attendance was approximately 90%.  The State of New Hampshire's recently released 
average was approximately 92.8%.  Dr. Espinola noted that the most comparable State data she could 
readily locate from earlier years was from 2021–2022.  At that time: 
 Manchester's average daily attendance was approximately 87.1%; and 
 the statewide average was approximately 90.9%. 
 
Manchester had therefore improved by approximately three percentage points since that time. 
 
Questions and comments included: 
1. Committee Member Stewart asked whether the 90% figure included excused and unexcused 
absences. Dr. Espinola confirmed that all absences were included. 
2. The Committee discussed the distinction among average daily attendance, chronic absenteeism, 
and truancy.  Dr. Espinola explained that every absence matters when evaluating chronic 
absenteeism, even when the District knows why the student is not present. 
3. Examples of chronic absenteeism could include: 
 illness; 
 suspension; 
 death in the family; or 
 other known circumstances. 
4. Truancy is different because the student is absent without a known or appropriate explanation. 
5. Dr. Espinola also noted that the distinction between excused and unexcused absences can 
sometimes be imperfect because a parent may call a student in sick without medical 
documentation.  For extended illness exceeding approximately 20 days, the District generally 
requests medical documentation so staff can better support the student.  
6. Committee Member Taylor clarified that average daily attendance represents the approximate 
percentage of students physically present in school on a typical day.  Dr. Espinola confirmed that 
interpretation. 
7. Committee Member Taylor requested historical data that would allow the Committee to compare 
attendance patterns over multiple years.  He noted that changes in District policy make it 
important to understand whether attendance patterns have improved or declined over time.  Dr.
August 19, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 8 of 9 
 
Espinola stated that prior reports were not always calculated in the same manner, which made 
direct comparisons difficult.  She agreed to make an effort to reconstruct comparable historical 
data where possible. 
8. Committee Member St. John requested that future reports show the percentage of students who 
are chronically absent.  He stated that a 90% average daily attendance rate can appear positive 
while masking the number of individual students missing a significant percentage of the school 
year. 
9. The Committee agreed that chronic absenteeism provides a different and important measure of 
student attendance. 
10. Chair Hamer noted that chronic absenteeism may have been the earlier statistic Committee 
Member Stewart had recalled. 
11. Committee Member Stewart clarified that the approximately 69% figure she remembered from an 
earlier discussion had related to chronic absenteeism rather than unexcused absences.  Dr. 
Espinola agreed to provide chronic absenteeism data beginning with the September report. 
12. Committee Member St. John also requested that quarterly reports identify the percentage of 
students who are on track to become chronically absent, rather than waiting until the end of the 
school year to determine which students met the threshold. He suggested using the proportion of 
absences accumulated at each point in the year to identify students who are trending toward 
chronic absenteeism. 
 
 
11. NEW BUSINESS 
 
Committee Chair Hamer confirmed that individual schools would continue working on their ABC goals. 
Dr. Espinola confirmed that each school would continue establishing goals related to attendance, behavior, 
and curriculum.  She explained that goals may differ by school based upon the needs of the student 
population. For example, one school might have relatively strong attendance and therefore set a modest 
attendance-improvement goal while establishing a more ambitious curriculum goal.  Another school might 
need to make attendance its primary focus before significant curriculum gains could reasonably be 
expected.  The Committee stated that this flexibility would allow schools to address their most significant 
needs while remaining aligned with overall District priorities.
August 19, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 9 of 9 
 
ADJOURNMENT 
 
12. If there is no further business, a motion is in order to adjourn.  
 
 
 
On motion of Committee Member Want, duly seconded by Committee Member St. John, it was moved to 
adjourn.  All were in favor, meeting adjourned at 5:27 p.m.
